body.text: Recommendation feeds and sharing features can expose harmful content to people beyond the original audience. As more users view, comment on, or share the content, online abuse can spread quickly and reach larger audiences.

Harmful comments on videos can remain visible long after they are posted, allowing abuse to continue over time. During livestreams, abusive messages can appear and multiply rapidly as viewers react in real time.

Replies, reposts, and mentions can spread abusive messages across public conversations. When many users join in, a single harmful comment can develop into repeated or coordinated attacks against an individual.

Harmful comments can spread within online communities as members respond, share, or encourage similar behaviour. Group discussions may reinforce negative attitudes and lead to repeated abuse targeting the same person.

Abusive messages can be forwarded or shared between individuals and groups, spreading harmful content through private conversations. Limited visibility outside these spaces can make it difficult to identify and address ongoing abuse.

html.text:
Matteo is a high-performing college volleyball athlete with ambitions of joining the national team.

Between demanding coursework and intensive training, he has been under considerable pressure and struggling to stay focused.

During an important match, Matteo serves into the net on match point, costing his team the match. The crowd reacts strongly, and some spectators begin shouting harsh criticism about his performance from the stands. The reaction continues as Matteo leaves the court.

Is this online abuse? No.

The criticism may be aggressive and harmful, but this is still happening offline. However, reactions that begin at a sporting event / on the ground, can quickly move into digital spaces, where they may reach a much wider audience.

After the match, the criticism moves online. A fan posts a video of Matteo’s missing serve, tags Matteo’s social media account, and adds insulting and humiliating comments intended to ridicule him.

The situation has become online abuse.

The fan is using insulting and humiliating content directed at Matteo through a digital platform. This is offensive speech.

By the next day, many users had joined in. Hostile comments are appearing across Matteo’s social media accounts, and the video of his missed serve is being repeatedly shared alongside insulting posts.

The situation has escalated to digital hostility.

What began with one user has developed into a repeated and collective pattern of hostile online interactions.

i1.text: Online abuse takes different forms. Offensive speech, hate speech, and digital hostility help us recognise different ways harmful behaviour can appear and develop online.

i2.text: Context matters. Consider the language being used, who or what is being targeted, and the pattern of interactions when identifying online abuse.

i3.text: Different forms of abuse can overlap. A single interaction may involve more than one behaviour, and its characteristics can change as the situation develops.

i4.text: Online abuse can escalate. A single harmful post can develop into repeated or collective hostility as others comment, share, repost, or amplify the content.

i5.text: Some people face disproportionate risk. Identity, visibility, role, and other contextual factors can affect who is targeted and the nature or intensity of the abuse they experience.

i6.text: Recognition is the first step towards action. Understanding what online abuse looks like helps people identify harmful situations and respond more effectively.

body.text: High public visibility can make athletes frequent targets of online abuse. Hateful reactions may arise from sporting outcomes, public perceptions, or interpretations of an athlete’s performance, actions, or personal decisions. These reactions can escalate quickly, allowing harmful content to spread across digital platforms.

Officials can face online abuse following decisions made during competition, adding to the verbal and physical abuse they may already experience in person. Repeated criticism, threats, and hostility can contribute to stress and affect their confidence, perceived authority, and wellbeing.

Journalists play an important role in connecting athletes, teams, and sporting organisations with wider audiences. Journalists may become targets of online hostility in response to their reporting, commentary or perceived position on an issue.

Sporting organisations and the people who fund, manage, and represent them can also become targets of online abuse. Hostile content may be directed at an organisation itself, its decisions, policies or actions, or at individual staff and representatives. This can affect organisational reputation, professional activity, decision-making, and the wellbeing of those involved.

The effects of online abuse can extend to the families and loved ones of those targeted. They may witness the abuse and its impact, become indirect targets through their association with the person experiencing abuse, or receive harmful messages directed at them personally. These experiences can also increase concern and fear for the safety and wellbeing of someone close to them.

Fans are the largest group in sport and are often overlooked. They can be affected by the abuse they encounter within sporting communities, even when they are not a direct target. Identity-based abuse aimed at an athlete, official, or other public figure can also affect fans who share that identity, contributing to an environment in which they may feel unwelcome or unsafe.

For athletes, these experiences may also raise concerns about their reputation, career opportunities, relationships with family and friends, and team performance. When abuse occurs publicly, its visibility and potential spread can further intensify psychological distress.

body.text: Online abuse can disrupt sleep and recovery. Harmful online experiences can continue beyond the initial interaction, affecting an athlete’s ability to rest and recover.

research.text: In a study of 912 young athletes aged 12–24, 10.4% reported experiencing online abuse. Among those affected, 44.3% reported moderate to severe effects on their sleep quality.

body.text: Online abuse often targets a person's abilities, body, or identity. Repeated criticism, including comments shared publicly to humiliate or hurt someone, can affect the targeted person's confidence and make them doubt their skills, decisions, and place in sport.

research.text: Research suggests that internal factors can shape how people respond to online hate. In a study of 60 public figures, including Olympic athletes, and 1,128 internet users, higher resilience and self-esteem were associated with lower levels of concern about the online hate they received. This suggests that people can experience the same type of hostility differently, depending in part on their psychological resources.

source.text: Jędryczka, W., Sorokowski, P., & Dobrowolska, M. (2022). The role of victim's resilience and self-esteem in experiencing internet hate. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health.

body.text: Threats and hostility online can extend concerns about safety beyond digital spaces. People targeted may worry about their own safety at home, during competition, and in public spaces. When threats also involve those close to them, these concerns can extend to family members and loved ones.

body.text: The detrimental effects of psychological stress on focus and performance are well documented. Because online abuse can cause mental distress, it can thus negatively affect the focus and performance of sportpeople, making it harder to concentrate, make decisions under pressure, and perform consistently.

i1.text: Online abuse can have wide-ranging effects. Its impact can extend across wellbeing, confidence, sense of safety, performance, participation, and other areas of a person’s life.

i2.text: The effects can be interconnected. Emotional distress, disrupted sleep, reduced confidence, safety concerns, and difficulties with focus can overlap and influence one another.

i3.text: People can be affected differently. Personal and contextual factors can shape how someone experiences and responds to online abuse.

i4.text: The impact extends beyond those directly targeted. Families, teammates, colleagues, fans, organisations, and others across sporting communities can also experience its consequences.

i5.text: Online abuse can affect participation and sporting culture. Persistent hostility can influence who feels safe, welcome, and able to participate in sport.

i6.text: The consequences can extend beyond sport. When discriminatory and abusive behaviours become normalised, they can reinforce prejudice, exclusion, and hostility in wider society.

section1Body.text: Pochopení toho, jak online zneužívání ovlivňuje lidi, nám pomáhá budovat empatii k těm, kterých se týká, a reagovat s péčí a respektem. Dopady online zneužívání na lidi mohou být závažné a dalekosáhlé: jediný příspěvek může v někom zanechat pocit úzkosti, nebezpečí nebo pochybnosti o sobě i dlouho po první interakci. Jak zneužívání pokračuje nebo se šíří napříč digitálními platformami, jeho dopad se může zesílit. Online zneužívání může ovlivnit duševní zdraví a pohodu, stejně jako výkony sportovců, přístup funkcionářů k rozhodnutím a to, jak novináři a další profesionálové přistupují ke své práci. Tyto dopady se mohou rozšířit i za osobu, která je terčem zneužívání. Rodiny, spoluhráči, kolegové a fanoušci mohou být svědky nebo zažít důsledky zneužívání. V širším smyslu může přetrvávající online nepřátelství formovat sportovní kulturu, ovlivňovat účast a ovlivňovat, kdo se ve sportu cítí bezpečně a vítán.
section1Body.note: Section body on Online Abuse in Sport: The Human Impact

section2Body.text: Známí sportovci čelí velkému množství online zneužívání. Sportovci však nejsou jedinými cílovými skupinami.
section2Body.note: Section body on Online Abuse in Sport: The Human Impact

section3Body.text: Online zneužívání může postihnout každého, kdo se zabývá sportem. Jeho důsledky se liší v závislosti na jednotlivci a jeho okolnostech, přičemž některé dopady jsou obzvláště relevantní pro sportovce. Tyto účinky se mohou také vzájemně posilovat: úzkost může narušit spánek, špatný spánek může ovlivnit soustředění a sebevědomí a tyto kombinované účinky mohou ovlivnit každodenní činnosti, sportovní výkon a celkovou pohodu.
section3Body.note: Section body on Online Abuse in Sport: The Human Impact

section4Body.text: Poté, co sportovec opakovaně dostával online urážlivé zprávy, začal méně často zveřejňovat příspěvky na sociálních sítích. Jeho trenér si všiml, že se během tréninku jeví roztržitě, a nedávno zmínil, že špatně spí a má úzkost z účasti na veřejných akcích.
section4Body.note: Section body on Online Abuse in Sport: The Human Impact

section5Body.text: Dopady online zneužívání se mohou projevovat i mimo jednotlivce a formovat kulturu sportu a komunit v jeho okolí. Rozšířené nepřátelství může ovlivnit to, kdo se cítí vítán, bezpečně a kdo se může účastnit, s důsledky pro začleňování a udržitelnost sportovních komunit. Sport má také širší společenský vliv. Chování a postoje projevované ve sportovních prostorách mohou přispívat k širším společenským normám. Když se diskriminační nebo zneužívající chování stane normalizovaným, může posílit předsudky, vyloučení a nepřátelství i mimo sport.

What it can cover: Conduct that constitutes a criminal offence under the applicable law, which may include certain threats, stalking, hate crimes, or non-consensual sharing of intimate images.

Who takes action: Law enforcement may investigate, and the relevant prosecuting authority determines whether a case proceeds.

Possible outcomes: Criminal penalties can include fines or imprisonment, depending on the offence and jurisdiction.

example.text:
Following a decision during a match, a referee begins receiving repeated messages in their social media from the same account. The messages become increasingly threatening and include references to seriously harming the referee and members of their family.

Depending on the applicable law and circumstances, threats of this nature could lead to a report to law enforcement and a criminal investigation.

imageAlt.text: Athlete facing circulating online claims and a lost sponsorship

pathway.text:
What it can cover: Disputes involving legal rights between individuals or organisations, which may include defamation, harassment, misuse of private information, or other privacy-related claims.

Who takes action: The person or organisation bringing the claim initiates the legal process.

Possible outcomes: Depending on the applicable law, remedies can include compensation or court orders requiring particular conduct to stop.

example.text:
False allegations about an athlete begin circulating online and are repeatedly shared. The claims damage the athlete’s professional reputation, and a sponsor ends its relationship with them after seeing such allegations.

Depending on the applicable law and circumstances, the athlete may be able to bring a civil claim seeking a remedy for the harm caused, including orders for removal of existing false content, injunctions to prevent further publication, monetary claims against the perpetuator if identifiable etc..

pathway.text:
What it can cover: Legal obligations enforced by regulators, including rules applying to online services or the handling of personal data.

Who takes action: Relevant regulatory authorities oversee and enforce these requirements. Individuals and organisations may also be able to submit complaints.

Possible outcomes: Regulators may investigate, require changes, or impose penalties where the applicable law gives them those powers.

example.text:
An athlete discovers that their personal contact information has been published online without their permission. The information continues to circulate, creating concerns about their privacy and safety.

Depending on the applicable data protection rules, the athlete or their organisation may be able to raise the matter with the relevant regulatory authority.

html.text: Online abuse can cross national borders immediately. The person targeted, the person responsible, and the platform may all be located in different jurisdictions, with different laws and enforcement processes.

Accounts may use pseudonyms, false identities, or limited identifying information, making it difficult to determine who is responsible for particular behaviour. Identifying an account holder can require information held by platforms and, in some cases, formal legal processes.

The volume and speed of online activity can make investigation and enforcement difficult. Available resources, specialist expertise, evidentiary requirements, and enforcement priorities can all affect what happens after an incident is reported.

Each harmful or abusive behaviour does not automatically constitute a legal offence or give rise to a legal claim. The applicable legal definition, evidence, context, and jurisdiction all matter.

This means that legal action is one part of the response to online abuse. Policies of the online platforms and the sporting organisations’ own standards and policies can also help address certain behaviours that may not have enough grounds for a legal action.

html.text:
In the UK, several laws address harmful online conduct. The Online Safety Act 2023 introduces offences relating to threatening communications, cyberflashing, and sharing or threatening to share intimate images without consent. The Protection from Harassment Act 1997 also covers harassment and stalking, including conduct involving digital communications. The Online Safety Act additionally places duties on regulated platforms to address illegal content and protect children from harmful material. The applicable protections depend on the conduct and jurisdiction.

Source: Legislation.gov.uk

In the United States, online abuse is addressed through a combination of federal and state laws. Federal legislation, including 18 U.S.C. 2261A, addresses certain forms of cyberstalking involving electronic communications. Other federal provisions cover threats and specific forms of online harassment, while state laws may provide additional protections against cyberbullying, harassment, stalking, and non-consensual sharing of intimate images. Legal definitions, enforcement, and available remedies vary by jurisdiction and the circumstances of each case.

Source: U.S. Code

Czech law does not rely on a single offence of “online abuse”. Existing legislation can apply to specific harmful behaviours carried out online. For example, Section 354 of the Czech Criminal Code (Act No. 40/2009 Coll.) addresses stalking, including conduct carried out through electronic communications. Czech Police guidance on stalking explains this provision and identifies repeated social media messages, threats, misuse of personal data, and reputational attacks among behaviours that may occur in stalking cases.

The Czech Civil Code (Act No. 89/2012 Coll.) also protects personality rights, including a person’s dignity, honour and privacy. A person affected by unlawful interference can seek to have the interference stopped and its consequences remedied.

Source: e-Sbírka

Spain’s Criminal Code (Organic Law 10/1995) addresses several forms of online abuse. Article 172 ter covers stalking, including repeated unwanted contact, misuse of personal data and the creation of fake social-media profiles using someone’s image without consent when this causes harassment or humiliation.

Article 510 addresses online hate speech, with increased penalties for certain offences when digital platforms make the content accessible to a large audience.

Victims can report suspected offences to the Spanish National Police or Civil Guard (Guardia Civil). Additional support is available through INCIBE’s free, confidential 017 helpline, while the Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) provides a Priority Channel for requesting the urgent removal of unlawfully shared sexual or violent content.

Source: Gobierno de España

In Sweden, online hate or abuse is not a separate legal category. The Swedish Police explains that the same criminal laws generally apply to conduct online as they do offline, with relevant offences potentially including unlawful threats, harassment, defamation, insult, unlawful invasion of privacy, sexual harassment, unlawful identity misuse (e.g. fake profiles in someone else's name), and agitation against a population group. If an offence is motivated by, for example, the victim's ethnicity, religion or sexual orientation, this is an aggravating circumstance in sentencing.

Swedish law also recognises unlawful persecution, which can arise from repeated criminal acts against the same person. Police guidance specifically advises people experiencing stalking to preserve emails, text messages, call records and other digital communications as potential evidence.

Sources: polisen.se; Swedish Parliament

Slovenian law addresses online abuse through existing legislation covering specific harmful behaviours. A particularly relevant example is Article 134a of the Slovenian Criminal Code (KZ-1), which defines stalking to include repeated attempts to establish unwanted contact through electronic communications, where the conduct causes fear or a sense of threat. Slovenian authorities have also recognised the online dimension of stalking in guidance concerning the application of this provision.

Slovenian Police guidance recognises online violence as including behaviours such as threats, harassment, spreading false or insulting content, misuse of photographs, impersonation and the creation of harmful fake profiles. Whether particular conduct constitutes a criminal offence depends on the circumstances of the individual case.

Source: GOV.SI

intro.text:

title.text: What each of us can do

body.text:
For athletes and others with public-facing roles:

  • Manage your exposure. Review privacy and safety settings and control who can contact, mention, or tag you.
  • Use safety tools. Mute, restrict, block, and report harmful accounts or content.
  • Preserve evidence. Save relevant information when behaviour may need to be reported or escalated.
  • Protect your wellbeing. You can choose to take a break from online interactions and seek support from people you trust.
Why does this matter?

Your wellbeing matters, and support is a shared responsibility. When people use safety and wellbeing tools, they are better equipped to prevent harm within the wider sporting community.
body.note: HTML allowed

body.text:
As a teammate, colleague, fan, friend, or bystander:

  • Avoid amplification. Prevent further circulation of abusive content.
  • Check in privately. Offer personal support to the person targeted.
  • Report appropriately. Take action through established channels, generally without public confrontation.
  • Speak up safely. Express concern about abusive behaviour or seek help from someone who can intervene, including organisational authorities or the police when necessary.
Why does this matter?

Supporting others strengthens the sporting community. Small actions from teammates, colleagues, friends, fans, and other bystanders can help create a social support system where people feel heard, protected, and cared for, and harmful behaviour is less likely to go unchallenged.

body.text:
When responding to online abuse, consider the situation, personal safety, and whether additional support is needed:

  • Assess the situation. Consider the nature of the behaviour, whether it is escalating, and whether anyone may be at risk.
  • Avoid unsafe engagement. Do not confront or engage directly when doing so could increase harm or place someone at risk.
  • Know when to seek support. Involve a trusted person or the appropriate organisational contact when the situation requires additional help.
  • Escalate safety concerns. Threats, repeated unwanted contact, exposure of personal information, or other safety concerns may require further organisational or external support.
Why does this matter?

Acting safely helps connect individual action with the right level of support. Recognising when a situation requires additional help allows others to become involved and helps ensure that safety remains the priority.

Education can shape how people understand online behaviours, while shared standards and laws can clarify expectations, research can identify emerging risks, and technology can influence how harmful content spreads.

title.text: Mini Dictionary: Other Possible Forms of Online Abuse

fullText.text:
Mini Dictionary: Other Possible Forms of Online Abuse
Toxic Content
* Purposeful embarrassment - Intentionally causing someone shame or humiliation, often publicly.
* Cyberbullying - Repeated use of electronic communication to intimidate, scare, or shame a person.
* Trolling - Posting provocative or offensive messages to trigger strong reactions or disrupt discussion.
* Profane or offensive content - Vulgar or disrespectful language, images, or communication.
* Threats of violence - Messages meant to create fear of physical harm.
* Incitement - Urging others to act violently or unlawfully.
* Sexual harassment - Unwanted sexual advances or comments.
* Unwanted explicit content - Sharing sexually explicit images or messages without consent.
Content Leakage
* Sextortion - Blackmail that threatens to release private material unless demands are met.
* Doxxing - Publishing private or identifying information with malicious intent.
* Outing - Disclosing someone's sexuality or gender identity without permission.
* Deadnaming - Using a transgender or non-binary person's former name without consent.
* Non-consensual image exposure - Sharing private or intimate images or videos without consent.
* Leaked chats or profiles - Exposing private conversations or accounts without authorisation.
Overloading
* System or account flooding - Overwhelming a person or platform with excessive content or requests to disrupt service or silence speech.
* Zoombombing - Uninvited intrusion into a video call to disrupt it.
* Negative ratings and reviews - Coordinated unfair or biased feedback meant to damage a reputation.
False Reporting
* Swatting - A hoax emergency call meant to trigger an armed police response at someone's location.
* Falsified abuse report - Knowingly submitting a false report to cause harm.
* Falsified abuse flag - Wrongly flagging legitimate content as abusive to have it removed or censored.
Impersonation
* Impersonated profiles - Fake accounts created to deceive or defraud.
* Impersonated chats or images - Fabricated or altered content falsely attributed to someone.
* Synthetic pornography - Deepfake technology used to create explicit content without consent.
* Impersonated web pages - Counterfeit sites built to deceive users or harm a competitor's standing.
* Hijacked communication - Unauthorised takeover of an account or channel to spread false messages.
Surveillance
* Stalking or tracking - Repeated, unwanted monitoring of a person's movements or activity.
* Account monitoring - Unauthorised access to and tracking of someone's account activity.
* Device monitoring - Unauthorised tracking of activity on a person's phone, computer, or tablet.
* IoT monitoring - Passive data collection from wearables or smart devices without consent.
* Browser monitoring - Tracking someone's browsing history or activity without their knowledge.
Lockout and Control
* Content deletion - Unauthorised removal of files, posts, or data to suppress information or cause harm.
* Browser or device hijacking - Taking control of someone's browser or connected devices without consent.
* Account lockouts - Deliberately blocking a person from accessing their own accounts or content.

body.text: Sport spojuje miliony lidí napříč zeměmi, kulturami a generacemi prostřednictvím vášně, hrdosti a vzrušení ze soutěžení. Online zneužívání toto spojení ohrožuje. Když jsou sportovci, funkcionáři, dobrovolníci a fanoušci online napadáni za to, kým jsou nebo jak podávají výkony, následky mohou sahat daleko za hranice obrazovky – zraňovat lidi, narušovat kariéru a normalizovat zneužívající chování. Organizace United Against Online Abuse (UAOA) sdružuje více než 75 vlád, sportů, akademiků a technologických platforem kolem společného cíle: učinit sport bezpečnějším před online zneužíváním. Trvalá změna vyžaduje akci napříč institucemi, komunitami a jednotlivci, a to zahrnuje i vás. Hlavním cílem iniciativy UAOA, vyvinuté ve spolupráci s Univerzitou Notre Dame, je tento e-learningový kurz, jehož hlavním cílem je pomoci vám rozpoznat různé formy online zneužívání, pochopit jejich dopad na vaši sportovní komunitu a s jistotou používat postupy hlášení. Po absolvování vás tento kurz připraví na informované kroky a přispění k bezpečnějšímu sportovnímu prostředí. Děkujeme, že jste se k tomuto úsilí připojili.

buildReadinessBody.text: Povědomí je jen začátek. Tento kurz rozvíjí praktické znalosti a dovednosti potřebné k pochopení online zneužívání a k přijetí informovaných opatření pro sebe i pro vaši sportovní komunitu. Kurz je navržen tak, aby vám pomohl s jakýmkoli chápáním tématu: Pokud již znáte online zneužívání, prohloubete své znalosti systémů hlášení, digitálních platforem, umělé inteligence a nových přístupů k prevenci a reakci. Pokud je pro vás téma nové, vybudujte si pevný základ a identifikujte praktické způsoby, jak přispět k bezpečnějším online praktikám a digitálním prostorům ve sportu. Po absolvování kurzu budete lépe vybaveni k rozpoznání online zneužívání, k sebevědomé reakci a k ​​aktivní roli při vytváření bezpečnějšího sportu.

body.text: Délka kurzuPřibližně 90 minut, absolvování vlastním tempem.Pro koho je kurz určen?Pro každého, kdo se účastní sportu, pracuje ve sportu nebo se jím angažuje a chce lépe porozumět online zneužívání a reagovat na něj, včetně sportovců, trenérů, funkcionářů, zaměstnanců, dobrovolníků, administrátorů, mediálních profesionálů, fanoušků a dalších osob v celé sportovní komunitě.Co můžete očekávat?Pět krátkých modulů kombinuje praktické rady, scénáře a příležitosti k aplikaci toho, co se naučíte. Nejsou vyžadovány žádné předchozí znalosti o online zneužívání.
